# About this document {.unnumbered}

This document is a reference analysis for the author, not a course page. It shows what
students could do with these data with the tools of Chapters 1 to 7 (RTMB, RTMBdist,
DHARMa and TMB), and follows the structure of the infiltration analysis in
`Case Studies/Infiltration/` and of Case study 2: the data, an exploration, the model, the
choice of curve, variance and random effect, the candidates for the effects of temperature
and water, the answer, checks of the model and a simulation of the estimator.
Alternatives are in boxes titled "Alternative" and traps in boxes titled "Pitfall";
@sec-summary lists them all. `README.md` in this folder describes what is known and not
known about the data.

::: {.callout-note title="Possible research question (for the author to decide)"}
How does the growth temperature (22 °C or 28 °C) change the light response of
photosynthesis of *Arabidopsis* (its maximum rate $p_{\max}$, initial slope $\alpha$,
curvature $\theta$ and dark respiration $r_d$), and does a week of drought change it, alone
or together with the growth temperature? All curves were measured at the same temperature,
so differences between the growth temperatures are acclimation, not the direct effect of
temperature on the measurement. The answer below gives the typical value of each parameter
in each combination of temperature and water, and the ratios between the combinations.
:::

The document needs RTMB, RTMBdist, DHARMa, TMB and knitr and takes about two minutes to
render, most of it in the simulation of @sec-simulation. The optimisations are
deterministic and every simulation has its own seed. Numbers in the text are calculated
inline from the code, except descriptions of what a figure shows, which were written from
the figures of the run of 20 November 2026 (R 4.6.1).

Status: generated draft, not reviewed by the author.

# The data {#sec-data}

The file contains 243 measurements of net photosynthesis (`P`, µmol/m²/s of CO₂) at a
given light intensity (`I`, µmol/m²/s of photons) on 27 light response curves
(`Replicate`), measured on plants grown at a low or a high temperature (`T`: `LT`, 22 °C;
`HT`, 28 °C), watered every other day (`W`: `C`, control) or not watered for 7 days before
the measurement (`D`, drought), in five batches (`Batch`).

```{r}
photo = read.csv("PhotosynthesisArabidopsisRaw.csv")
str(photo)
```

We store the treatments as factors with the low temperature and the control as reference
levels. The column `T` is renamed: `T` is also R's abbreviation of `TRUE`, which makes code
that uses it hard to read. Each value of `Replicate` is one curve (they are numbered 1 to
27 across batches), so `Curve` is a factor of it, and `Combination` names the four
combinations of temperature and water.

```{r}
photo$Temperature = factor(photo$T, levels = c("LT", "HT"))
photo$Water = factor(photo$W, levels = c("C", "D"))
photo$Batch = factor(photo$Batch)
photo$Curve = factor(photo$Replicate)
photo$Combination = interaction(photo$Temperature, photo$Water, sep = "-")
levels(photo$Combination)

# Colours (Okabe-Ito) and symbols of the four combinations, colours of the five batches.
combination_colours = c("#0072B2", "#D55E00", "#009E73", "#E69F00")
combination_symbols = c(1, 19, 2, 17)
batch_colours = c("#000000", "#E69F00", "#56B4E9", "#009E73", "#CC79A7")

# Formatting of numbers quoted in the text.
f1 = function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1)
f2 = function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2)
f3 = function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 3)
```

# Exploratory data analysis {#sec-eda}

## The design {#sec-design}

Temperature, water and batch are properties of the curve, so we first make a table with one
row per curve and count the curves in each batch and combination.

```{r}
curve_info = photo[!duplicated(photo$Curve),
                   c("Curve", "Batch", "Temperature", "Water", "Combination")]
rownames(curve_info) = NULL
n_curves = table(curve_info$Batch, curve_info$Combination)
n_curves
colSums(n_curves)
```

Every batch has one curve of HT-C and one of HT-D. LT-C has two or three curves per batch
(`r colSums(n_curves)[["LT-C"]]` in all) and LT-D one or two, with none in batch 4. The
design is a two-by-two factorial in five batches, unbalanced towards the low-temperature
controls.

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall: the number of curves, not of measurements"}
Temperature and water are properties of the plant, so the information about their effects
comes from 27 curves, not from 243 measurements, and from only five curves in each of the
combinations HT-C, LT-D and HT-D.
:::

Each curve has nine measurements at the same nominal light intensities, from 25 to 1000
µmol/m²/s, and the recorded intensities differ from the nominal ones by hundredths of a
µmol/m²/s at most:

```{r}
table(table(photo$Curve))
table(round(photo$I))
max(abs(photo$I - round(photo$I)))
```

The rows of each curve are sorted from low to high light, which is also the order in which
the light levels were applied; the leaf was kept at each level for 5 to 8 minutes before
the reading (README).

## Light response curves {#sec-curves}

@fig-curves shows each curve as a line, one panel per combination, coloured by batch.

```{r}
#| label: fig-curves
#| fig-cap: "Net photosynthesis against light intensity, one line per curve and one
#|   panel per combination of growth temperature (LT, HT) and water (C, control; D,
#|   drought). The colour shows the batch."
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 6
old_par = par(no.readonly = TRUE)
par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
for (g in levels(photo$Combination)) {
  photo_g = photo[photo$Combination == g, ]
  plot(P ~ I, data = photo_g, type = "n", ylim = range(photo$P), main = g,
       xlab = "Light intensity (µmol/m²/s)",
       ylab = "Net photosynthesis (µmol/m²/s)")
  abline(h = 0, lty = 3)
  for (j in unique(as.character(photo_g$Curve))) {
    photo_j = photo_g[photo_g$Curve == j, ]
    lines(P ~ I, data = photo_j, type = "b", pch = 19, cex = 0.5,
          col = batch_colours[photo_j$Batch[1]])
  }
}
legend("bottomright", legend = paste("Batch", levels(photo$Batch)),
       col = batch_colours, lty = 1, bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
par(old_par)
```

Every curve rises almost linearly at low light and bends towards a plateau, which none of
them reaches by 1000 µmol/m²/s. The curves are smooth: the measurements of a curve deviate
little from a smooth line, while curves of the same combination differ by up to a factor
of two at high light. Compared with the low-temperature controls (LT-C), the plants grown
at the high temperature (HT-C) reach lower rates and differ less among themselves. Drought
seems to change little at the low temperature (LT-D) but lowers the rates at the high
temperature (HT-D), and by very different amounts in different plants: the two lowest
HT-D curves are those of batches 1 and 2. One LT-C curve of batch 1 levels off far below
the others.

## Low light and respiration {#sec-low-light}

The data have no measurement in the dark, so dark respiration can only be estimated by
extending the curves to zero light. At 25 µmol/m²/s some net rates are negative (the leaf
releases more CO₂ by respiration than it fixes):

```{r}
low = photo[round(photo$I) == 25, ]
sum(low$P < 0)
tapply(low$P, low$Combination, mean)
```

`r sum(low$P < 0)` of the 27 curves have a negative rate at the lowest light. A first
estimate of the initial slope of each curve is the change in rate between 25 and 50
µmol/m²/s divided by the change in light, and extending this line to zero light gives a
first estimate of the dark respiration:

```{r}
first_two = split(photo[round(photo$I) %in% c(25, 50), ], ~ Curve)
initial_slope = sapply(first_two, function(x) diff(x$P) / diff(x$I))
respiration_line = sapply(first_two, function(x) x$I[1] * diff(x$P) / diff(x$I) - x$P[1])
summary(initial_slope)
summary(respiration_line)
```

The initial slopes are around `r f2(median(initial_slope))` (µmol of CO₂ per µmol of
photons), and the line through the first two points crosses zero light at a rate of about
−`r f1(median(respiration_line))` µmol/m²/s. Because the curves already bend between 25
and 50 µmol/m²/s, the slope of this line is lower than the initial slope of the curve, and
the respiration it gives is lower too.

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall: respiration is an extrapolation"}
Every estimate of $r_d$ in this document is the value of a curve extended from 25
µmol/m²/s to zero light, so it depends on the shape that the curve assumes below the
lowest measurement. In the leaf, respiration in the light can also differ from respiration
in the dark (a known effect at low light in leaf physiology). A light response curve with a
measurement in the dark would test this.
:::

## The spread among curves {#sec-spread-among}

For each combination and light level we calculate the mean and the standard deviation of
the rates across curves (@fig-spread-among).

```{r}
#| label: fig-spread-among
#| fig-cap: "Standard deviation against mean of the rates across the curves of a
#|   combination, at each of the nine light levels."
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 4
light_level = round(photo$I)
among_mean = tapply(photo$P, list(light_level, photo$Combination), mean)
among_sd = tapply(photo$P, list(light_level, photo$Combination), sd)
matplot(among_mean, among_sd, pch = combination_symbols, col = combination_colours,
        xlab = "Mean rate across curves (µmol/m²/s)",
        ylab = "Standard deviation (µmol/m²/s)")
legend("topleft", legend = levels(photo$Combination), pch = combination_symbols,
       col = combination_colours, bty = "n")
# Coefficients of variation from 100 umol/m2/s upwards.
round(among_sd / among_mean, 2)[-(1:2), ]
```

In LT-C and HT-D the standard deviation across curves grows in proportion to the mean
rate, with coefficients of variation of about 0.16 and 0.33 from 100 µmol/m²/s upwards:
the curves differ by a factor (a curve that is high at one light level is high at every
light level), by a larger one in HT-D, where the drought affected some plants much more
than others. In HT-C and LT-D the standard deviation stays between about 0.3 and 0.9
µmol/m²/s and even falls at the highest light levels, so these curves differ more in the
middle of the light range than at its end, a difference in shape. At the lowest light the
standard deviation does not fall to zero with the mean, because the curves differ in their
respiration. With five curves in three of the combinations, each standard deviation is
itself uncertain. On the whole, the figure suggests a random effect that multiplies the
whole curve, including the respiration (@sec-model), and @sec-choices compares it with
other placements. It also suggests that the plants of some combinations differ more than
those of others (@sec-sd-combination).

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall: the spread among curves is not the measurement error"}
@fig-spread-among shows how the curves differ from each other, which the random effect
describes. The error of a gas exchange measurement, which could also depend on the flux,
is the deviation of each measurement from the curve of its own leaf, and the figure says
nothing about it. @sec-one-curve looks at it.
:::

## Batches {#sec-batches}

The rate at the highest light (1000 µmol/m²/s) summarises each curve without a model. Its
mean per batch and combination:

```{r}
high = photo[round(photo$I) == 1000, ]
round(tapply(high$P, list(high$Batch, high$Combination), mean), 1)
```

Batch 1 is lowest or close to the lowest in LT-C and HT-C, but the differences between
batches are small compared with the spread within LT-C (@fig-curves), except for HT-D,
where the rate of batches 1 and 2 is about half that of batches 3 and 4. With one HT-D
curve per batch, we cannot tell whether the drought was more severe in those batches (for
example because the soil dried faster) or whether these plants simply responded more. The
data contain no measure of soil water or plant water status (README).

# The two curves {#sec-curve-functions}

The non-rectangular hyperbola (functions supplement, `sec-fn-nonrectangular`) describes
the gross rate of photosynthesis of a leaf as a function of light $I$:

$$
f(I) = \frac{\alpha I + p_{\max} - \sqrt{(\alpha I + p_{\max})^2 - 4\,\theta\,\alpha I\,p_{\max}}}{2\,\theta},
$$

where $\alpha$ is the initial slope (µmol of CO₂ per µmol of photons, so without units),
$p_{\max}$ the asymptote (µmol/m²/s) and $\theta$ the sharpness of the bend ($0 < \theta
\leq 1$). The saturating exponential (`sec-fn-monomolecular`), $a\left(1 - e^{-bI}\right)$
with the asymptote $a = p_{\max}$ and the initial slope $ab = \alpha$, has the same two
parameters with the same meaning:

$$
f(I) = p_{\max}\left(1 - e^{-\alpha I / p_{\max}}\right).
$$

The net rate that the instrument measures is the gross rate minus the dark respiration
$r_d$ (µmol/m²/s), so both models of the net rate are $f(I) - r_d$, and the measured rate
at zero light would be $-r_d$.

The formula of the non-rectangular hyperbola divides by $\theta$, and the curves of
@sec-one-curve put $\theta$ close to zero. When $\theta$ is small, the numerator is the
difference of two nearly equal numbers, and rounding error makes the result inaccurate.
Multiplying numerator and denominator by $\alpha I + p_{\max} + \sqrt{\cdots}$ gives the
same function in a form without this problem:

$$
f(I) = \frac{2\,\alpha I\,p_{\max}}{\alpha I + p_{\max} + \sqrt{(\alpha I + p_{\max})^2 - 4\,\theta\,\alpha I\,p_{\max}}},
$$

which at $\theta = 0$ is the Michaelis–Menten function $\alpha I\,p_{\max}/(\alpha I +
p_{\max})$. We use this form.

```{r}
library(RTMB)
library(RTMBdist)

# Gross rate of the two curves.
nrh_rate = function(I, alpha, pmax, theta) {
  s = alpha * I
  2 * s * pmax / (s + pmax + sqrt((s + pmax)^2 - 4 * theta * s * pmax))
}
mono_rate = function(I, alpha, pmax) {
  pmax * (1 - exp(-alpha * I / pmax))
}

# The textbook form, for comparison.
nrh_textbook = function(I, alpha, pmax, theta) {
  s = alpha * I
  (s + pmax - sqrt((s + pmax)^2 - 4 * theta * s * pmax)) / (2 * theta)
}
theta_values = c(0.5, 1e-4, 1e-8, 1e-12, 1e-14)
print(rbind(textbook = nrh_textbook(500, 0.06, 12, theta_values),
            stable = nrh_rate(500, 0.06, 12, theta_values)), digits = 7)
```

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall: rounding error in the textbook formula"}
At $\theta = 10^{-12}$ the textbook formula gives
`r formatC(nrh_textbook(500, 0.06, 12, 1e-12), format = "f", digits = 4)` µmol/m²/s
instead of `r formatC(nrh_rate(500, 0.06, 12, 1e-12), format = "f", digits = 4)`, and at
$10^{-14}$ `r formatC(nrh_textbook(500, 0.06, 12, 1e-14), format = "f", digits = 4)`:
the error grows as $\theta$ approaches zero. An optimiser that moves $\theta$ towards zero
then works with a likelihood that is distorted by rounding error, and its gradients are
unreliable. Students who copy the formula from a paper will meet this as soon as a fit
puts $\theta$ near zero, which happens with these data.
:::

# One curve at a time {#sec-one-curve}

## A fit for each curve

To see how far the measurements of a curve deviate from a smooth curve, we fit the
non-rectangular hyperbola to each curve on its own, with Normal deviations of constant
standard deviation (no pooling, in the terms of Chapter 7). The parameters are estimated on
the log scale ($\alpha$, $p_{\max}$, $r_d$, $\sigma_{\mathrm{obs}}$) and the logit scale
($\theta$). The starting values are read from @fig-curves and @sec-low-light: an initial
slope of 0.05, an asymptote of 12 µmol/m²/s (above the highest rates, as the curves still
rise), a respiration of 1 µmol/m²/s, $\theta = 0.5$ and a standard deviation of 1
µmol/m²/s.

```{r}
# Connect a likelihood to a data set.
cmb = function(f, d) function(p) f(p, d)

single_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  mu = nrh_rate(I, exp(log_alpha), exp(log_pmax), plogis(logit_theta)) - exp(log_rd)
  -sum(dnorm(x = P, mean = mu, sd = exp(log_sd_obs), log = TRUE))
}

fit_single = function(curve_data, start) {
  obj = MakeADFun(cmb(single_nll, curve_data), start, silent = TRUE)
  fit = optim(par = obj$par, fn = obj$fn, gr = obj$gr, method = "BFGS")
  list(obj = obj, fit = fit)
}

single_start = list(log_alpha = log(0.05), log_pmax = log(12), logit_theta = 0,
                    log_rd = log(1), log_sd_obs = log(1))
curve_names = levels(photo$Curve)
single_fits = list()
for (j in curve_names) {
  rows = photo$Curve == j
  single_fits[[j]] = fit_single(list(I = photo$I[rows], P = photo$P[rows]),
                                single_start)
}
single_sd = sapply(single_fits, function(f) exp(f$fit$par[["log_sd_obs"]]))
collapsed = curve_names[single_sd > 1]
collapsed
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
# How many fits collapse when the standard deviation starts at 0.1 instead of 1.
small_start = single_start
small_start$log_sd_obs = log(0.1)
n_collapsed_small = 0
for (j in curve_names) {
  rows = photo$Curve == j
  f = fit_single(list(I = photo$I[rows], P = photo$P[rows]), small_start)
  n_collapsed_small = n_collapsed_small + (exp(f$fit$par[["log_sd_obs"]]) > 1)
}
```

All fits except `r if (length(collapsed) == 1) "one" else length(collapsed)` end with a
standard deviation between
`r f2(min(single_sd[!(curve_names %in% collapsed)]))` and
`r f2(max(single_sd[!(curve_names %in% collapsed)]))` µmol/m²/s. The fit of curve `r collapsed` (HT-D, batch 1, the lowest curve) ends with
$\alpha$ and $p_{\max}$ near zero and a standard deviation of
`r f1(single_sd[collapsed])` µmol/m²/s: the optimiser gave up on the curve and explains the
rates by noise. We refit it from starting values read from its own measurements (the
initial slope and respiration of @sec-low-light, and its highest rate as asymptote):

```{r}
for (j in collapsed) {
  rows = photo$Curve == j
  start_j = single_start
  start_j$log_alpha = log(initial_slope[[j]])
  start_j$log_pmax = log(max(photo$P[rows]))
  start_j$log_rd = log(max(respiration_line[[j]], 0.1))
  single_fits[[j]] = fit_single(list(I = photo$I[rows], P = photo$P[rows]), start_j)
}
single_sd = sapply(single_fits, function(f) exp(f$fit$par[["log_sd_obs"]]))
round(single_sd[collapsed], 3)
```

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall: fits of single curves collapse"}
With the same starting values for every curve, `r length(collapsed)` of 27 fits stopped at
a flat curve, and with a starting standard deviation of 0.1 µmol/m²/s instead of 1,
`r n_collapsed_small` did. A small starting standard deviation makes the misfit of the
starting curve very costly, the first step of BFGS is then very long and can land where the
curve has disappeared. Large starting standard deviations, and starting values read from
each curve, avoid this. The mixed models below are less sensitive, because the
distribution of the curve effects keeps every curve near the others.
:::

## The deviations within curves {#sec-within}

The residuals of these fits are the deviations of the measurements from the curve of their
own leaf (@fig-within).

```{r}
single_par = t(sapply(single_fits, function(f) f$fit$par))
photo$single_fitted = NA
for (j in curve_names) {
  rows = photo$Curve == j
  p = single_par[j, ]
  photo$single_fitted[rows] = nrh_rate(photo$I[rows], exp(p[["log_alpha"]]),
                                       exp(p[["log_pmax"]]), plogis(p[["logit_theta"]])) -
    exp(p[["log_rd"]])
}
photo$single_residual = photo$P - photo$single_fitted
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-within
#| fig-cap: "Residuals of the fits to single curves against the fitted rate (left) and
#|   against the light intensity (right)."
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 3.4
old_par = par(no.readonly = TRUE)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
plot(single_residual ~ single_fitted, data = photo, xlab = "Fitted rate (µmol/m²/s)",
     ylab = "Residual (µmol/m²/s)")
abline(h = 0, lty = 3)
plot(single_residual ~ I, data = photo, xlab = "Light intensity (µmol/m²/s)",
     ylab = "Residual (µmol/m²/s)")
abline(h = 0, lty = 3)
par(old_par)
fitted_class = cut(photo$single_fitted, breaks = c(-2, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 13))
round(tapply(photo$single_residual, fitted_class, sd), 3)
round(tapply(photo$single_residual, round(photo$I), sd), 3)
```

The residuals are small (standard deviation about `r f2(sd(photo$single_residual))`
µmol/m²/s, against differences of several µmol/m²/s between curves) and their spread does
not change systematically with the fitted rate or with the light intensity; the larger
standard deviation at 500 µmol/m²/s comes from one measurement that lies about 0.5
µmol/m²/s below its curve. So the exploration does not support a standard deviation that
changes with the flux; we nevertheless compare a constant standard deviation with one that
changes with the expected rate in @sec-choices. These residuals underestimate the measurement error somewhat (each
curve has five parameters for nine points), but this affects all fitted rates alike.

## The parameters of the curves {#sec-single-parameters}

@fig-single-parameters shows the estimates of the four parameters of each curve.

```{r}
single = data.frame(
  Combination = curve_info$Combination,
  Batch = curve_info$Batch,
  alpha = exp(single_par[, "log_alpha"]),
  pmax = exp(single_par[, "log_pmax"]),
  theta = plogis(single_par[, "logit_theta"]),
  rd = exp(single_par[, "log_rd"])
)
round(sapply(single[, c("alpha", "pmax", "theta", "rd")], summary), 3)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-single-parameters
#| fig-cap: "Estimates of the parameters of each curve, fitted on its own, by
#|   combination: initial slope, asymptote and dark respiration (log scales) and
#|   sharpness of the bend."
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 5.5
old_par = par(no.readonly = TRUE)
par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
parameter_labels = c(alpha = "Initial slope alpha", pmax = "p_max (µmol/m²/s)",
                     rd = "r_d (µmol/m²/s)", theta = "theta")
for (p in names(parameter_labels)) {
  stripchart(single[[p]] ~ single$Combination, vertical = TRUE,
             log = if (p == "theta") "" else "y", method = "jitter", jitter = 0.1,
             pch = combination_symbols, col = combination_colours,
             xlab = "Combination", ylab = parameter_labels[[p]])
}
par(old_par)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
n_theta_zero = sum(single$theta < 0.01)
theta_others = range(single$theta[single$theta >= 0.01])
rd_zero = as.character(single$Combination[single$rd < 0.01])
```

Three things stand out.

- **$\theta$ is poorly determined by one curve.** In `r n_theta_zero` of the 27 curves it
  is below 0.01, at the boundary of its range (the Michaelis–Menten shape), and in the
  others it is spread between `r f2(theta_others[1])` and `r f2(theta_others[2])`. Nine
  points per curve, none of them beyond the bend, cannot tell a sharp bend from a gradual
  one.
- **Temperature and drought.** The asymptotes of HT-C lie below those of LT-C, those of
  LT-D overlap with LT-C, and HT-D spreads from the lowest values to the range of LT-C. The
  initial slopes are similar except in HT-D. In `r length(rd_zero)` curves
  (`r paste(rd_zero, collapse = " and ")`) the respiration is estimated at practically
  zero.
- **The parameters vary together.** Within each combination, the logarithms of $\alpha$,
  $p_{\max}$ and $r_d$ are positively correlated:

```{r}
centred = sapply(single[, c("alpha", "pmax", "rd")],
                 function(x) log(x) - ave(log(x), single$Combination))
round(cor(centred), 2)
```

A curve with a high asymptote tends to have a high initial slope and a high respiration,
which is what a random effect that multiplies the whole net curve assumes. The correlations
are far from one, so the shapes of the curves differ too (@sec-two-re).

## What we take forward {#sec-forward}

- **The curve:** the non-rectangular hyperbola or the saturating exponential, minus the
  dark respiration, written with $\alpha$ and $p_{\max}$ in both.
- **The measurements:** Normal deviations from the curve of their leaf, with a constant
  standard deviation; one that changes with the expected rate as an alternative.
- **The groups:** the 27 curves; they differ mostly by a factor, so a random effect that
  multiplies the whole curve (alternatives: only $p_{\max}$, or the gross rate without
  respiration).
- **The predictors:** temperature, water and their interaction, properties of the curve,
  through model matrices built from one row per curve (Chapter 7, `sec-model-matrix`); the
  batch as a block.
- **Not modelled:** differences in the shape of the curves (@sec-two-re), the order of the
  measurements within a curve (@sec-serial) and the water status of the plants (README).

# The model {#sec-model}

## The model for the measurements

The model for measurement $i$ of curve $j$, with the non-rectangular hyperbola, a constant
standard deviation and the random effect on the whole net curve, is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\log(\alpha_j) &= \beta_{\alpha,0} + \beta_{\alpha,\mathrm{H}}\,H_j + \beta_{\alpha,\mathrm{D}}\,D_j
  + \beta_{\alpha,\mathrm{HD}}\,H_j D_j + u_j,\\
\log(p_{\max,j}) &= \beta_{p,0} + \beta_{p,\mathrm{H}}\,H_j + \beta_{p,\mathrm{D}}\,D_j
  + \beta_{p,\mathrm{HD}}\,H_j D_j + u_j,\\
\log(r_{d,j}) &= \beta_{r,0} + \beta_{r,\mathrm{H}}\,H_j + \beta_{r,\mathrm{D}}\,D_j
  + \beta_{r,\mathrm{HD}}\,H_j D_j + u_j,\\
\operatorname{logit}(\theta) &= \beta_{\theta},\\
u_j &\sim \operatorname{Normal}(0, \sigma^2_{\mathrm{curve}}),\\
\mu_{ij} &= f(I_{ij}; \alpha_j, p_{\max,j}, \theta) - r_{d,j},\\
P_{ij} \mid u_j &\sim \operatorname{Normal}(\mu_{ij}, \sigma^2_{\mathrm{obs}}),
\end{aligned}
$$

where $H_j$ is 1 if plant $j$ grew at the high temperature and 0 otherwise, $D_j$ is 1 if
it was droughted, $I_{ij}$ is the light intensity of the measurement, $f$ is the gross rate
of @sec-curve-functions, and the measurements are independent for given $u_j$. The same
$u_j$ in the first three lines multiplies the whole net curve of plant $j$ by $e^{u_j}$:
the gross rate is multiplied by $e^{u_j}$ when $\alpha$ and $p_{\max}$ both are, because
$f(I; e^u\alpha, e^u p_{\max}, \theta) = e^u f(I; \alpha, p_{\max}, \theta)$ for both
curves. A difference in leaf properties that scales every flux of the leaf (for example in
the amount of photosynthetic machinery per unit of leaf area) would have this effect. An
error in the leaf area is excluded here, because every leaf filled the 6 cm² chamber.

The variable-variance alternative replaces $\sigma_{\mathrm{obs}}$ by
$\sigma_{\mathrm{obs}}\,e^{\delta\mu_{ij}}$, so that the standard deviation changes by a
factor $e^{\delta}$ for each µmol/m²/s of expected rate. It contains the constant standard
deviation at $\delta = 0$, inside the range of $\delta$, and it works for expected rates
near zero or negative, where a standard deviation proportional to a power of the mean would
not.

The typical curve of a combination ($u_j = 0$) is that of its median plant. The answer
gives the typical $\alpha$, $p_{\max}$ and $r_d$ of each combination and four ratios:
HT/LT in the controls and in drought (the effect of the growth temperature), and drought
over control at each temperature (the effect of drought).

## Implementation

The NLL needs the index of the curve of each measurement (1 to 27), the treatments of each
curve (`curve_info`, for the model matrices of the curves) and the four combinations
(`combinations`, one row per combination, for the typical values).

```{r}
curve_index = as.numeric(photo$Curve)
combinations = data.frame(
  Temperature = factor(c("LT", "HT", "LT", "HT"), levels = c("LT", "HT")),
  Water = factor(c("C", "C", "D", "D"), levels = c("C", "D"))
)
rownames(combinations) = levels(photo$Combination)
comparisons = c("HT/LT, control", "HT/LT, drought", "D/C, LT", "D/C, HT")

photo_data = list(I = photo$I, P = photo$P, curve_id = curve_index)
```

One joint NLL covers every model of this document. Four choices are elements of the list
of data:

- `curve_type`: `"NRH"` (non-rectangular hyperbola) or `"mono"` (saturating exponential);
- `variance`: `"constant"` or `"exponential"` ($\sigma_{\mathrm{obs}}\,e^{\delta\mu}$);
- `random_on`: `"pmax"` (the random effect multiplies $p_{\max}$ only), `"gross"` (it
  multiplies $\alpha$ and $p_{\max}$, so the gross rate) or `"net"` (it multiplies
  $\alpha$, $p_{\max}$ and $r_d$, so the whole net curve);
- `use_batch`: `TRUE` adds a block effect of the batch that multiplies the whole net curve,
  like the random effect but the same for all curves of a batch.

A fifth element, the model matrix `X_sd`, lets the standard deviation among curves depend
on the combination (@sec-sd-combination); with the formula `~ 1` it is one standard
deviation for all curves, as in Chapter 7.

`ADREPORT()` gives the logarithms of the typical $\alpha$, $p_{\max}$ and $r_d$, the logit
of the typical $\theta$ and the logarithm of the typical net rate at 1000 µmol/m²/s, for
each combination, and the four log ratios of each of $\alpha$, $p_{\max}$ and $r_d$. With
batches, the typical values are those of an average batch (the mean of the five batch
effects on the log scale).

```{r}
photo_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  P = OBS(P)
  # Minus the log density of the deviations of the curves, before they are used.
  sd_curve = exp(X_sd %*% log_sd_curve)
  nll = -sum(dnorm(x = u, mean = 0, sd = sd_curve, log = TRUE))
  # Where the deviations act, and the block effect of the batches.
  u_alpha = u
  u_rd = u
  if (random_on == "pmax") u_alpha = 0 * u
  if (random_on != "net") u_rd = 0 * u
  block = 0 * u
  block_typical = 0
  if (use_batch) {
    block = X_batch %*% beta_batch
    block_typical = sum(beta_batch) / (length(beta_batch) + 1)
  }
  # Parameters of each curve and typical parameters (u = 0) of each combination.
  alpha_curve = exp(X_alpha %*% beta_alpha + u_alpha + block)
  pmax_curve = exp(X_pmax %*% beta_pmax + u + block)
  rd_curve = exp(X_rd %*% beta_rd + u_rd + block)
  log_alpha = X_alpha_typical %*% beta_alpha + block_typical
  log_pmax = X_pmax_typical %*% beta_pmax + block_typical
  log_rd = X_rd_typical %*% beta_rd + block_typical
  # Expected rate of each measurement and typical rate at 1000 umol/m2/s.
  alpha_i = alpha_curve[curve_id]
  pmax_i = pmax_curve[curve_id]
  if (curve_type == "NRH") {
    theta_curve = plogis(X_theta %*% beta_theta)
    mu = nrh_rate(I, alpha_i, pmax_i, theta_curve[curve_id]) - rd_curve[curve_id]
    logit_theta = X_theta_typical %*% beta_theta
    gross_1000 = nrh_rate(1000, exp(log_alpha), exp(log_pmax), plogis(logit_theta))
    ADREPORT(logit_theta)
  } else {
    mu = mono_rate(I, alpha_i, pmax_i) - rd_curve[curve_id]
    gross_1000 = mono_rate(1000, exp(log_alpha), exp(log_pmax))
  }
  log_p1000 = log(gross_1000 - exp(log_rd))
  # Log ratios: HT/LT in C and in D, D/C at LT and at HT.
  log_ratio_alpha = log_alpha[c(2, 4, 3, 4)] - log_alpha[c(1, 3, 1, 2)]
  log_ratio_pmax = log_pmax[c(2, 4, 3, 4)] - log_pmax[c(1, 3, 1, 2)]
  log_ratio_rd = log_rd[c(2, 4, 3, 4)] - log_rd[c(1, 3, 1, 2)]
  ADREPORT(log_alpha)
  ADREPORT(log_pmax)
  ADREPORT(log_rd)
  ADREPORT(log_p1000)
  ADREPORT(log_ratio_alpha)
  ADREPORT(log_ratio_pmax)
  ADREPORT(log_ratio_rd)
  # Minus the log density of the measurements for given deviations.
  sd_obs = exp(log_sd_obs)
  if (variance == "exponential") sd_obs = exp(log_sd_obs + delta * mu)
  nll - sum(dnorm(x = P, mean = mu, sd = sd_obs, log = TRUE))
}
```

`photo_setup()` builds the list of data and the starting values for a list of formulas
(for $\alpha$, $p_{\max}$, $\theta$ and $r_d$) and the four choices. The baselines are those
of @sec-one-curve, every effect starts at zero, $\sigma_{\mathrm{obs}}$ at 0.5 µmol/m²/s,
$\delta$ at zero and $\sigma_{\mathrm{curve}}$ at 0.2 (curves differ by about 20%,
@sec-spread-among). The formula for $\theta$ is ignored for the saturating exponential.

```{r}
photo_setup = function(formulas, curve_type, variance, random_on, use_batch = FALSE,
                       sd_formula = ~ 1) {
  data = photo_data
  data$curve_type = curve_type
  data$variance = variance
  data$random_on = random_on
  data$use_batch = use_batch
  data$X_sd = model.matrix(sd_formula, data = curve_info)
  for (p in c("alpha", "pmax", "theta", "rd")) {
    data[[paste0("X_", p)]] = model.matrix(formulas[[p]], data = curve_info)
    data[[paste0("X_", p, "_typical")]] = model.matrix(formulas[[p]], data = combinations)
  }
  data$X_batch = model.matrix(~ Batch, data = curve_info)[, -1]
  baseline = c(alpha = 0.05, pmax = 12, rd = 1)
  start = list()
  for (p in names(baseline)) {
    start[[paste0("beta_", p)]] = c(log(baseline[[p]]),
                                    rep(0, ncol(data[[paste0("X_", p)]]) - 1))
  }
  if (curve_type == "NRH") {
    start$beta_theta = c(qlogis(0.5), rep(0, ncol(data$X_theta) - 1))
  }
  start$log_sd_obs = log(0.5)
  if (variance == "exponential") start$delta = 0
  if (use_batch) start$beta_batch = rep(0, ncol(data$X_batch))
  start$log_sd_curve = rep(log(0.2), ncol(data$X_sd))
  list(data = data, start = start)
}
```

Three helpers complete the toolkit:

- `fit_photo()` processes the joint NLL for one list of data, integrating out `u`, and
  minimises it;
- `aic_table()` reports, for a named list of fits, $K$, the log-likelihood, the convergence
  code, the largest absolute gradient at the solution, AIC and the difference from the
  lowest AIC;
- `photo_answer()` gives the typical $\alpha$, $p_{\max}$ and $r_d$ of each combination,
  the typical $\theta$ and net rate at 1000 µmol/m²/s, and the four ratios of $\alpha$,
  $p_{\max}$ and $r_d$, with Wald intervals calculated on the log (or logit) scale and
  transformed back.

```{r}
fit_photo = function(data, start) {
  start$u = rep(0, nlevels(photo$Curve))
  obj = MakeADFun(cmb(photo_nll, data), start, random = "u", silent = TRUE)
  fit = optim(par = obj$par, fn = obj$fn, gr = obj$gr, method = "BFGS")
  list(obj = obj, fit = fit)
}

aic_table = function(fits) {
  out = data.frame(
    model = names(fits),
    K = sapply(fits, function(f) length(f$fit$par)),
    loglik = sapply(fits, function(f) -f$fit$value),
    convergence = sapply(fits, function(f) f$fit$convergence),
    max_gradient = sapply(fits, function(f) max(abs(f$obj$gr(f$fit$par))))
  )
  out$aic = 2 * out$K - 2 * out$loglik
  out$delta_aic = out$aic - min(out$aic)
  rownames(out) = NULL
  out
}

critical_value = qnorm(p = 0.975)
photo_answer = function(obj) {
  report = summary(sdreport(obj), select = "report")
  # Estimates and Wald intervals of the rows called name, transformed back.
  back = function(name, inverse = exp) {
    rows = rownames(report) == name
    estimate = report[rows, "Estimate"]
    se = report[rows, "Std. Error"]
    data.frame(estimate = inverse(estimate),
               lower = inverse(estimate - critical_value * se),
               upper = inverse(estimate + critical_value * se))
  }
  typical = list(alpha = back("log_alpha"), pmax = back("log_pmax"),
                 rd = back("log_rd"), p1000 = back("log_p1000"))
  if ("logit_theta" %in% rownames(report)) {
    typical$theta = back("logit_theta", plogis)
  }
  ratios = list(alpha = back("log_ratio_alpha"), pmax = back("log_ratio_pmax"),
                rd = back("log_ratio_rd"))
  list(typical = typical, ratios = ratios)
}

# An estimate with its interval, as text, and a table of them.
with_interval = function(tab, digits = 2) {
  paste0(formatC(tab$estimate, format = "f", digits = digits), " (",
         formatC(tab$lower, format = "f", digits = digits), " to ",
         formatC(tab$upper, format = "f", digits = digits), ")")
}
show_table = function(tab, digits = 2) {
  if ("max_gradient" %in% names(tab)) {
    tab$max_gradient = format(signif(tab$max_gradient, 2))
  }
  knitr::kable(tab, digits = digits, row.names = FALSE)
}
```

# Which curve, which variance, which random effect? {#sec-choices}

The full model lets temperature, water and their interaction change every parameter of the
curve, so that the comparison is not affected by effects that we left out. Two curves, two
models of the variance and three placements of the random effect make twelve fits.

```{r}
full_formulas = list(alpha = ~ Temperature * Water, pmax = ~ Temperature * Water,
                     theta = ~ Temperature * Water, rd = ~ Temperature * Water)

choices = expand.grid(curve_type = c("NRH", "mono"),
                      variance = c("constant", "exponential"),
                      random_on = c("pmax", "gross", "net"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
choice_fits = list()
for (i in seq_len(nrow(choices))) {
  setup = photo_setup(full_formulas, choices$curve_type[i], choices$variance[i],
                      choices$random_on[i])
  choice_fits[[i]] = fit_photo(setup$data, setup$start)
}
names(choice_fits) = paste(choices$curve_type, choices$variance, choices$random_on)
choice_table = aic_table(choice_fits)
show_table(choice_table[order(choice_table$aic), ], digits = 1)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
# AIC differences quoted in the text.
aic_choice = setNames(choice_table$aic, choice_table$model)
mono_gap = aic_choice[["mono constant net"]] - aic_choice[["NRH constant net"]]
pmax_gap = aic_choice[["NRH constant pmax"]] - aic_choice[["NRH constant net"]]
gross_gap = aic_choice[["NRH constant gross"]] - aic_choice[["NRH constant net"]]
variance_gap = aic_choice[["NRH exponential net"]] - aic_choice[["NRH constant net"]]
delta_net = choice_fits[["NRH exponential net"]]$fit$par[["delta"]]
full_report = summary(sdreport(choice_fits[["NRH constant net"]]$obj), select = "report")
theta_full = plogis(full_report[rownames(full_report) == "logit_theta", "Estimate"])
```

`r if (all(choice_table$convergence == 0)) "All twelve fits converged." else "Not every fit converged (see the table)."`
The non-rectangular hyperbola beats the saturating exponential by `r round(mono_gap)` AIC
units (with constant variance and the random effect on the net curve), as the sharper bend
of the saturating exponential does not fit the gradual approach to the plateau. The random
effect on the whole net curve is the best placement: `r f1(gross_gap)` units better than
on the gross rate and `r round(pmax_gap)` units better than on $p_{\max}$ only, as
@sec-spread-among and @sec-single-parameters suggested.

The standard deviation that changes with the expected rate does not improve the fit: with
the non-rectangular hyperbola and the random effect on the net curve, $\delta$ is
`r f3(delta_net)` and AIC is `r f1(variance_gap)` units worse than with a constant
standard deviation. So, as in @sec-within, the data give no support for a variance that
grows with the flux. We continue with the non-rectangular hyperbola, a constant standard
deviation and the random effect on the whole net curve.

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall: the curvature at the boundary"}
In the full model, the typical $\theta$ of the high-temperature combinations goes to the
boundary (`r paste(formatC(theta_full, format = "g", digits = 2), collapse = ", ")` for
LT-C, HT-C, LT-D and HT-D), with enormous standard errors on the logit scale, while the
optimiser reports convergence (with the largest gradient of the table,
`r format(signif(choice_table$max_gradient[choice_table$model == "NRH constant net"], 2))`). Like the single curves of @sec-single-parameters, the
data cannot determine $\theta$ separately for each combination. @sec-candidates gives the
four combinations a common $\theta$.
:::

# Which parameters depend on temperature and water? {#sec-candidates}

With the non-rectangular hyperbola, a constant standard deviation and a random effect on
the whole net curve, the candidates have no effect of the treatments (`none`), effects of
temperature, water and their interaction on $p_{\max}$ only (`pmax`), on $p_{\max}$ and
$\alpha$ (`pmax_alpha`), on $p_{\max}$, $\alpha$ and $r_d$ with a common $\theta$
(`common_theta`) and on all four parameters (`full`); `additive` has effects of
temperature and water without interaction on $p_{\max}$, $\alpha$ and $r_d$.

```{r}
by_treatment = ~ Temperature * Water
additive = ~ Temperature + Water
common = ~ 1
candidates = list(
  none = list(alpha = common, pmax = common, theta = common, rd = common),
  pmax = list(alpha = common, pmax = by_treatment, theta = common, rd = common),
  pmax_alpha = list(alpha = by_treatment, pmax = by_treatment, theta = common,
                    rd = common),
  common_theta = list(alpha = by_treatment, pmax = by_treatment, theta = common,
                      rd = by_treatment),
  additive = list(alpha = additive, pmax = additive, theta = common, rd = additive),
  full = full_formulas
)
candidate_setups = list()
candidate_fits = list()
for (m in names(candidates)) {
  candidate_setups[[m]] = photo_setup(candidates[[m]], "NRH", "constant", "net")
  candidate_fits[[m]] = fit_photo(candidate_setups[[m]]$data,
                                  candidate_setups[[m]]$start)
}
candidate_table = aic_table(candidate_fits)
show_table(candidate_table, digits = 1)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
delta_cand = setNames(candidate_table$delta_aic, candidate_table$model)
best_candidate = candidate_table$model[which.min(candidate_table$aic)]
```

`r if (all(candidate_table$convergence == 0)) "All six fits converged." else "Not every fit converged (see the table)."`
The best candidate is `r best_candidate`. The treatments change more than the asymptote:
`pmax` is `r f1(delta_cand[["pmax"]])` AIC units behind, and `pmax_alpha`, which keeps a
common respiration, `r f1(delta_cand[["pmax_alpha"]])` units. The model without interaction
(`additive`) is `r f1(delta_cand[["additive"]])` units behind with
`r candidate_table$K[candidate_table$model == "common_theta"] - candidate_table$K[candidate_table$model == "additive"]`
parameters fewer, so the data support an interaction only weakly: the effect of drought
may or may not differ between the growth temperatures. Letting $\theta$ depend on the
treatments (`full`) costs `r f1(delta_cand[["full"]] - delta_cand[["common_theta"]])` units
compared with `common_theta`.

We take `common_theta` as the main model, because it is the best by AIC and because the
question asks how the effect of drought depends on the growth temperature, which needs the
interaction.

::: {.callout-tip title="Alternative"}
Report the additive model, in which the effect of drought is the same factor at both
temperatures. It is close in AIC, and its ratios have narrower intervals, but it cannot
answer whether drought matters more after growth at the high temperature.
:::

## The batches {#sec-batch}

The batch enters as a block effect that multiplies the whole net curve of every plant of a
batch, with batch 1 as the reference level:

```{r}
batch_setup = photo_setup(candidates$common_theta, "NRH", "constant", "net",
                          use_batch = TRUE)
batch_fit = fit_photo(batch_setup$data, batch_setup$start)
batch_table = aic_table(list(common_theta = candidate_fits$common_theta,
                             with_batch = batch_fit))
show_table(batch_table, digits = 1)
batch_effects = exp(batch_fit$fit$par[names(batch_fit$fit$par) == "beta_batch"])
names(batch_effects) = paste("Batch", 2:5)
round(batch_effects, 2)
```

The batches 2 to 5 have curves `r round(100 * (min(batch_effects) - 1))`% to
`r round(100 * (max(batch_effects) - 1))`% higher than batch 1, but the model with
batches is `r f1(batch_table$delta_aic[2])` AIC units worse than the model without
(@sec-sensitivity shows that it gives the same answer). The batch effect that matters in
@sec-batches, the low HT-D curves of batches 1 and 2, is an interaction of batch and
treatment that a block effect cannot describe, and with one HT-D curve per batch no model
can separate it from the variation among plants.

# The answer: the light response in each combination {#sec-answer}

We take the candidate `common_theta` and calculate its `sdreport()`.

```{r}
main_data = candidate_setups$common_theta$data
main_start = candidate_setups$common_theta$start
main = candidate_fits$common_theta
main_obj = main$obj
main_fit = main$fit
main_fit$convergence
main_sd = sdreport(main_obj)
main_answer = photo_answer(main_obj)
```

The typical parameters of each combination, with Wald intervals ($\alpha$ without units,
$p_{\max}$ and $r_d$ in µmol/m²/s):

```{r}
typical_table = data.frame(
  combination = rownames(combinations),
  alpha = with_interval(main_answer$typical$alpha, 3),
  p_max = with_interval(main_answer$typical$pmax, 1),
  r_d = with_interval(main_answer$typical$rd, 2)
)
show_table(typical_table)
```

The ratios between combinations:

```{r}
ratio_table = data.frame(
  comparison = comparisons,
  alpha = with_interval(main_answer$ratios$alpha),
  p_max = with_interval(main_answer$ratios$pmax),
  r_d = with_interval(main_answer$ratios$rd)
)
show_table(ratio_table)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
ty = main_answer$typical
ra = main_answer$ratios
theta_main = ty$theta[1, ]
```

**Growth temperature.** In the controls, the typical plant grown at 28 °C has a maximum
rate `r round(100 * (1 - ra$pmax$estimate[1]))`% lower than one grown at 22 °C
(`r f1(ty$pmax$estimate[2])` against `r f1(ty$pmax$estimate[1])` µmol/m²/s; ratio
`r with_interval(ra$pmax[1, ])`), and an initial slope
`r round(100 * (1 - ra$alpha$estimate[1]))`% lower (ratio
`r with_interval(ra$alpha[1, ])`), while its respiration is similar (ratio
`r with_interval(ra$rd[1, ])`). In drought the differences between the temperatures are
larger: the maximum rate at 28 °C is `r round(100 * (1 - ra$pmax$estimate[2]))`% lower
(`r with_interval(ra$pmax[2, ])`), the initial slope
`r round(100 * (1 - ra$alpha$estimate[2]))`% (`r with_interval(ra$alpha[2, ])`) and the
respiration `r round(100 * (1 - ra$rd$estimate[2]))`% (`r with_interval(ra$rd[2, ])`).

**Drought.** At 22 °C, a week without water hardly changes the typical curve: the ratios
D/C are `r f2(ra$pmax$estimate[3])` for $p_{\max}$, `r f2(ra$alpha$estimate[3])` for
$\alpha$ and `r f2(ra$rd$estimate[3])` for $r_d$, and every interval includes 1. At 28 °C,
drought lowers the maximum rate by `r round(100 * (1 - ra$pmax$estimate[4]))`%
(`r with_interval(ra$pmax[4, ])`), halves the initial slope
(`r with_interval(ra$alpha[4, ])`) and lowers the respiration by
`r round(100 * (1 - ra$rd$estimate[4]))`% (`r with_interval(ra$rd[4, ])`). The data do
not tell whether the plants at 28 °C are more sensitive to drought or whether their soil
dried faster (README).

**Curvature.** The common $\theta$ is `r f2(theta_main$estimate)` (Wald interval
`r f2(theta_main$lower)` to `r f2(theta_main$upper)`, calculated on the logit scale),
which @sec-theta-profile examines.

@fig-typical shows the typical curves over the measurements.

```{r}
#| label: fig-typical
#| fig-cap: "Measurements (points, coloured by batch) and typical curves (u = 0) of the
#|   four combinations under the main model."
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 6
light_grid = seq(from = 0, to = 1000, length.out = 200)
old_par = par(no.readonly = TRUE)
par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
for (g in 1:4) {
  photo_g = photo[as.numeric(photo$Combination) == g, ]
  plot(P ~ I, data = photo_g, ylim = range(photo$P), xlim = c(0, 1000), pch = 19,
       cex = 0.6, col = batch_colours[photo_g$Batch], main = rownames(combinations)[g],
       xlab = "Light intensity (µmol/m²/s)",
       ylab = "Net photosynthesis (µmol/m²/s)")
  lines(light_grid, nrh_rate(light_grid, ty$alpha$estimate[g], ty$pmax$estimate[g],
                             theta_main$estimate) - ty$rd$estimate[g], lwd = 2)
  abline(h = 0, lty = 3)
}
par(old_par)
```

The typical curves run through the middle of the measurements of LT-C, HT-C and LT-D. In
HT-D the typical curve runs between the two high curves (batches 3 and 4) and the two
lowest ones (batches 1 and 2), a compromise for a combination in which the plants differ
by more than a factor of two.

The variance components, on the scale of the measurements and among curves:

```{r}
variance_components = exp(main_fit$par[c("log_sd_obs", "log_sd_curve")])
variance_components
```

The measurements deviate from the curve of their plant with a standard deviation of
`r f2(variance_components[1])` µmol/m²/s, about
`r round(variance_components[1] / sd(photo$single_residual))` times the residual standard
deviation of the single fits of @sec-within. The difference is
the shape of the curves: a single random effect can make a curve higher or lower, but not
steeper at low light and flatter at high light, so the remaining differences in shape
count as deviations of the measurements (@sec-serial, @sec-two-re). The curves of a
combination differ by a factor with a standard deviation of `r f2(variance_components[2])`
on the log scale: the middle 95% of plants span a factor of about
`r f1(exp(2 * critical_value * variance_components[2]))`.

## The curvature {#sec-theta-profile}

A likelihood profile of $\operatorname{logit}(\theta)$, with its interval transformed
back (the warning of `confint()` that the chunk suppresses comes from the flat part of the
profile described below):

```{r}
#| warning: false
main_profile_theta = TMB::tmbprofile(main_obj, name = "beta_theta", trace = FALSE)
theta_ci = plogis(c(estimate = main_fit$par[["beta_theta"]],
                    confint(main_profile_theta)[1, ]))
theta_ci
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
# Lower limit of the interval of theta: zero when the profile never crosses the cutoff.
theta_lower = if (is.na(theta_ci[["lower"]])) "0" else f2(theta_ci[["lower"]])
```

`r if (is.na(theta_ci[["lower"]])) "The profile never falls by 1.92 below its maximum as $\\theta$ decreases, so \x60confint()\x60 gives no lower limit: the" else "The"`
likelihood profile interval of $\theta$ runs from `r theta_lower` to
`r f2(theta_ci[["upper"]])`. As $\theta \to 0$ the curve becomes a Michaelis–Menten
function, and the data fit that shape almost as well as the estimate. The data allow
anything from the Michaelis–Menten shape to a moderately sharp bend. $\theta$ is not part
of the comparison of the combinations, but it matters for the next point.

## How far beyond the data is $p_{\max}$? {#sec-pmax}

The asymptote $p_{\max}$ is the gross rate in unlimited light. From the quadratic equation
of the non-rectangular hyperbola (functions supplement), the light at which the gross rate
reaches a fraction $q$ of $p_{\max}$ is

$$
I_q = \frac{q\,p_{\max}\,(1 - \theta q)}{\alpha\,(1 - q)}.
$$

For the typical LT-C plant:

```{r}
light_fraction = function(q, alpha, pmax, theta) {
  q * pmax * (1 - theta * q) / (alpha * (1 - q))
}
light_fraction(c(0.5, 0.9, 0.95), ty$alpha$estimate[1], ty$pmax$estimate[1],
               theta_main$estimate)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
light_90 = light_fraction(0.9, ty$alpha$estimate[1], ty$pmax$estimate[1],
                          theta_main$estimate)
mono_fit = choice_fits[["mono constant net"]]
mono_answer = photo_answer(mono_fit$obj)
```

The typical LT-C plant reaches 90% of its $p_{\max}$ at about
`r round(light_90, -2)` µmol/m²/s, beyond the highest light of the measurements. Its
typical net rate at 1000 µmol/m²/s is `r f1(ty$p1000$estimate[1])` µmol/m²/s, against an
asymptote of the net rate of
`r f1(ty$pmax$estimate[1] - ty$rd$estimate[1])` µmol/m²/s ($p_{\max} - r_d$).

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall: the asymptote depends on the curve"}
The saturating exponential (in its full model with the random effect on the net curve)
gives a typical $p_{\max}$ of `r f1(mono_answer$typical$pmax$estimate[1])` µmol/m²/s for
LT-C, against `r f1(ty$pmax$estimate[1])` for the non-rectangular hyperbola, while both
give a typical net rate at 1000 µmol/m²/s of about
`r f1(mono_answer$typical$p1000$estimate[1])` and `r f1(ty$p1000$estimate[1])` µmol/m²/s.
The value of $p_{\max}$ is an extrapolation whose size depends on the curve and on
$\theta$, which the data barely determine (@sec-theta-profile). Ratios of $p_{\max}$
between combinations are more robust than its values (@sec-sensitivity). For comparisons
with the literature, a rate at a stated high light, inside the data, is safer. There is a
further reason for caution: the light levels were applied from low to high with 5 to 8
minutes at each, and at high light the stomata had probably not finished opening, so the
rates at the highest light, and with them $p_{\max}$, are probably somewhat underestimated
(README).
:::

# Checking the model {#sec-checks}

## Scaled quantile residuals {#sec-residuals}

We simulate 1,000 hypothetical samples (new curve deviations, then new measurements for
them) and compare each measurement with the typical curve of its combination.

```{r}
n_sim = 1000
photo_simulations = matrix(NA, nrow = length(main_data$P), ncol = n_sim)
set.seed(seed = 2228)
for (s in seq_len(n_sim)) {
  photo_simulations[, s] = main_obj$simulate(main_fit$par)$P
}

combination_of_row = as.numeric(photo$Combination)
photo_expected = nrh_rate(photo$I, ty$alpha$estimate[combination_of_row],
                          ty$pmax$estimate[combination_of_row], theta_main$estimate) -
  ty$rd$estimate[combination_of_row]

photo_residuals = DHARMa::createDHARMa(
  simulatedResponse = photo_simulations,
  observedResponse = main_data$P,
  fittedPredictedResponse = photo_expected
)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-dharma
#| fig-cap: "Scaled quantile residuals of the main model: quantile-quantile plot (left)
#|   and residuals against the predicted rate (right)."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5
plot(photo_residuals)
dispersion = DHARMa::testDispersion(photo_residuals, plot = FALSE)$statistic
dispersion
```

The quantile-quantile plot is close to the line, and the dispersion statistic is
`r f2(dispersion)`. In the right panel the upper and lower quartiles of the residuals move
slightly towards the median at high predicted rates: at high light the curves differ a
little less than a common factor implies, as for HT-C and LT-D in @fig-spread-among. As in
Chapter 6, the p-values that DHARMa prints on its
plots are not used for decisions. These residuals compare each measurement with the
distribution of all plants of its combination, so they mainly check the distribution of the
curve effects; the deviations within a curve are checked in @sec-serial.

@fig-dharma-light shows the residuals against light and combination.

```{r}
#| label: fig-dharma-light
#| fig-cap: "Scaled quantile residuals against light intensity (left) and combination
#|   (right)."
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 3.6
old_par = par(no.readonly = TRUE)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
DHARMa::plotResiduals(photo_residuals, form = photo$I)
DHARMa::plotResiduals(photo_residuals, form = photo$Combination)
par(old_par)
```

One residual per curve, from the sum of its measurements:

```{r}
curve_residuals = DHARMa::recalculateResiduals(photo_residuals, group = curve_index)
curve_scaled = residuals(curve_residuals)
names(curve_scaled) = curve_names
round(sort(curve_scaled), 3)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
lowest_two = names(sort(curve_scaled))[1:2]
lowest_curve = lowest_two[1]
describe_curve = function(j) {
  info = curve_info[curve_info$Curve == j, ]
  paste0("curve ", j, " (", info$Combination, ", batch ", info$Batch, ", residual ",
         f3(curve_scaled[[j]]), ")")
}
```

The residuals of the curves spread over the whole range. The two lowest are
`r describe_curve(lowest_two[1])`, the lowest curve of HT-D, and
`r describe_curve(lowest_two[2])`, the LT-C curve that levels off far below the others in
@fig-curves. Among 27 curves, about `r f1(27 * 0.05)` residuals below 0.05 are expected
and there are `r sum(curve_scaled < 0.05)`, which is not a clear disagreement.

## Successive measurements of the same curve {#sec-serial}

The residuals above come from new curve deviations, so the measurements of one curve share
their deviation. Removing the mean of each curve (on the Normal scale) leaves the variation
within curves; the correlation of each residual with the next one of the same curve
measures how much neighbouring measurements resemble each other.

```{r}
next_same_curve = c(photo$Curve[-1] == photo$Curve[-nrow(photo)], FALSE)
normal_residuals = qnorm(pmin(pmax(residuals(photo_residuals), 0.001), 0.999))
within_curve = normal_residuals - ave(normal_residuals, photo$Curve)
serial_cor = cor(within_curve[next_same_curve],
                 within_curve[which(next_same_curve) + 1])
serial_cor
```

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall: deviations that follow the shape of the curve"}
The correlation is `r f2(serial_cor)`. Within a curve, a measurement above the typical
shape is followed by another one above it: the deviations follow the shape of each plant's
curve, which a single random effect cannot describe. In @fig-curves the measurements of a
curve lie on a smooth line, so this is a difference in shape, not noise in the instrument.
The model treats these deviations as independent, so it may overstate the information that
each curve carries about the shape and give standard errors that are too small.
@sec-two-re fits a second random effect that describes much of the difference in shape,
and shows that the ratios and their intervals change little.
:::

## The variation among plants in each combination {#sec-sd-combination}

@fig-spread-among and the right panel of @fig-dharma-light suggest that the plants of LT-C
and HT-D differ more among themselves than those of HT-C and LT-D. A separate standard
deviation among curves for each combination needs only another model matrix, for the
logarithm of $\sigma_{\mathrm{curve}}$ (the formula `~ 0 + Combination` gives one column
per combination, so each coefficient is the log standard deviation of one combination):

```{r}
sd_setup = photo_setup(candidates$common_theta, "NRH", "constant", "net",
                       sd_formula = ~ 0 + Combination)
sd_fit = fit_photo(sd_setup$data, sd_setup$start)
sd_table = aic_table(list(common_sd = main, sd_by_combination = sd_fit))
show_table(sd_table, digits = 1)
sd_by_combination = exp(sd_fit$fit$par[names(sd_fit$fit$par) == "log_sd_curve"])
names(sd_by_combination) = levels(photo$Combination)
round(sd_by_combination, 3)
sd_answer = photo_answer(sd_fit$obj)
sd_ratio_table = data.frame(
  comparison = comparisons,
  alpha = with_interval(sd_answer$ratios$alpha),
  p_max = with_interval(sd_answer$ratios$pmax),
  r_d = with_interval(sd_answer$ratios$rd)
)
show_table(sd_ratio_table)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
sra = sd_answer$ratios
```

The separate standard deviations improve AIC by `r f1(sd_table$aic[1] - sd_table$aic[2])`
units with `r sd_table$K[2] - sd_table$K[1]` parameters more. The curves of HT-D differ by
a factor with a standard deviation of `r f2(sd_by_combination[["HT-D"]])` on the log scale,
those of LT-C by `r f2(sd_by_combination[["LT-C"]])`, and those of HT-C and LT-D by
`r f2(sd_by_combination[["HT-C"]])` and `r f2(sd_by_combination[["LT-D"]])`, estimates
from five curves each. The estimated ratios are practically the same as in the main
model, but their intervals change: those that involve only the low temperature or the
controls become narrower, and those that involve HT-D become wider. The effect of drought
on $p_{\max}$ at 28 °C now has the interval `r with_interval(sra$pmax[4, ])`, which
`r if (sra$pmax$upper[4] > 1) "includes 1" else "stays below 1"`.

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall: one variance among groups for groups that differ"}
A common $\sigma_{\mathrm{curve}}$ averages over combinations whose plants differ by very
different amounts. The intervals of comparisons with the most variable combination (HT-D)
are then too narrow and those of the least variable ones too wide. Drought at the high
temperature made the plants differ more, which is itself a result: some plants lost much
more photosynthetic capacity than others.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Alternative"}
Use the model with a standard deviation among curves for each combination as the main
model. It is better by AIC and its intervals reflect the different variability of the
combinations, but each standard deviation rests on five curves (twelve for LT-C), and the
model goes one step beyond Chapter 7.
:::

## Sensitivity of the answer {#sec-sensitivity}

The ratios of $p_{\max}$ and $\alpha$ under five alternatives: the model with batches
(@sec-batch), the full model with the saturating exponential (@sec-choices), the main model
without curve `r lowest_curve` (the lowest residual of @sec-residuals), the main model
with the variance that changes with the expected rate, and the model with a standard
deviation among curves for each combination (@sec-sd-combination).

```{r}
subset_curves = function(data, keep) {
  rows = data$curve_id %in% keep
  data$I = data$I[rows]
  data$P = data$P[rows]
  data$curve_id = match(data$curve_id[rows], keep)
  for (p in c("alpha", "pmax", "theta", "rd")) {
    data[[paste0("X_", p)]] = data[[paste0("X_", p)]][keep, , drop = FALSE]
  }
  data$X_batch = data$X_batch[keep, , drop = FALSE]
  data$X_sd = data$X_sd[keep, , drop = FALSE]
  data
}
keep = setdiff(seq_along(curve_names), as.numeric(lowest_curve))
without_fit = fit_photo(subset_curves(main_data, keep), main_start)
without_fit$fit$convergence

exponential_setup = photo_setup(candidates$common_theta, "NRH", "exponential", "net")
exponential_fit = fit_photo(exponential_setup$data, exponential_setup$start)

# Columns: main model, with batches, saturating exponential, without the lowest curve,
# exponential standard deviation, standard deviation among curves for each combination.
sensitivity_answers = list(
  main = main_answer,
  batch = photo_answer(batch_fit$obj),
  mono = mono_answer,
  drop_lowest = photo_answer(without_fit$obj),
  exp_sd = photo_answer(exponential_fit$obj),
  sd_comb = sd_answer
)
sensitivity = data.frame(
  ratio = c(paste("p_max", comparisons), paste("alpha", comparisons)),
  sapply(sensitivity_answers,
         function(a) c(a$ratios$pmax$estimate, a$ratios$alpha$estimate))
)
show_table(sensitivity)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
spread = apply(sensitivity[, -1], 1, function(x) max(x) - min(x))
```

The ratios move by at most `r f2(max(spread))` between the alternatives, less than the
widths of their intervals. The largest changes come from leaving out curve
`r lowest_curve`, which moves the ratios that involve HT-D towards 1, as expected when one
of five curves is removed. Every alternative tells the same story: lower capacity after
growth at 28 °C, little effect of drought at 22 °C and a larger one at 28 °C.

# Beyond the course: two random effects per curve {#sec-two-re}

Chapter 7 uses one random effect per group. Here each curve gets a second, independent
deviation $v_j$ of $\log(\alpha_j)$ only (standard deviation $\sigma_{\alpha}$), so that the
initial slope can vary relative to the rest of the curve: a curve can be steeper at low
light without being higher at high light. We fit it with the constant and with the
exponential standard deviation.

```{r}
photo_nll_2re = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  P = OBS(P)
  nll = -sum(dnorm(x = u, mean = 0, sd = exp(log_sd_curve), log = TRUE))
  nll = nll - sum(dnorm(x = v, mean = 0, sd = exp(log_sd_alpha), log = TRUE))
  alpha_curve = exp(X_alpha %*% beta_alpha + u + v)
  pmax_curve = exp(X_pmax %*% beta_pmax + u)
  rd_curve = exp(X_rd %*% beta_rd + u)
  mu = nrh_rate(I, alpha_curve[curve_id], pmax_curve[curve_id], plogis(beta_theta)) -
    rd_curve[curve_id]
  log_alpha = X_alpha_typical %*% beta_alpha
  log_pmax = X_pmax_typical %*% beta_pmax
  log_rd = X_rd_typical %*% beta_rd
  log_ratio_alpha = log_alpha[c(2, 4, 3, 4)] - log_alpha[c(1, 3, 1, 2)]
  log_ratio_pmax = log_pmax[c(2, 4, 3, 4)] - log_pmax[c(1, 3, 1, 2)]
  ADREPORT(log_ratio_alpha)
  ADREPORT(log_ratio_pmax)
  sd_obs = exp(log_sd_obs)
  if (variance == "exponential") sd_obs = exp(log_sd_obs + delta * mu)
  nll - sum(dnorm(x = P, mean = mu, sd = sd_obs, log = TRUE))
}

fit_2re = function(variance) {
  data = main_data
  data$variance = variance
  start = main_start
  if (variance == "exponential") start$delta = 0
  start$log_sd_alpha = log(0.2)
  start$u = rep(0, length(curve_names))
  start$v = rep(0, length(curve_names))
  obj = MakeADFun(cmb(photo_nll_2re, data), start, random = c("u", "v"), silent = TRUE)
  fit = optim(par = obj$par, fn = obj$fn, gr = obj$gr, method = "BFGS")
  list(obj = obj, fit = fit)
}
two_re = list(constant = fit_2re("constant"), exponential = fit_2re("exponential"))
table_2re = aic_table(list(one_random_effect = main,
                           two_random_effects = two_re$constant,
                           two_random_effects_exponential = two_re$exponential))
show_table(table_2re, digits = 1)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
par_2re = two_re$constant$fit$par
par_2re_exp = two_re$exponential$fit$par
sd_2re = exp(par_2re[c("log_sd_obs", "log_sd_curve", "log_sd_alpha")])
report_2re = summary(sdreport(two_re$exponential$obj), select = "report")
ratios_2re = exp(report_2re[, "Estimate"])
lower_2re = exp(report_2re[, "Estimate"] - critical_value * report_2re[, "Std. Error"])
upper_2re = exp(report_2re[, "Estimate"] + critical_value * report_2re[, "Std. Error"])
sd_at = function(mu) exp(par_2re_exp[["log_sd_obs"]] + par_2re_exp[["delta"]] * mu)
```

The second random effect improves AIC by
`r round(table_2re$aic[1] - table_2re$aic[2])` units with
`r table_2re$K[2] - table_2re$K[1]` parameter more, a far larger difference than any in
@sec-choices and @sec-candidates. The standard deviation of the measurements falls from
`r f2(variance_components[1])` to `r f2(sd_2re[1])` µmol/m²/s, half way to the
`r f2(sd(photo$single_residual))` µmol/m²/s of the single fits, and the initial slopes vary
among curves with a standard deviation of `r f2(sd_2re[3])` on the log scale, in addition
to the common factor (now `r f2(sd_2re[2])`).

The variance question now has a different answer. With two random effects, the
exponential standard deviation improves AIC by
`r f1(table_2re$aic[2] - table_2re$aic[3])` units, with $\delta =$
`r f3(par_2re_exp[["delta"]])`: the standard deviation falls from
`r f2(sd_at(0))` µmol/m²/s at an expected rate of zero to `r f2(sd_at(10))` at 10
µmol/m²/s. The deviations are larger at low rates, not at high ones. The single fits of
@sec-within did not show this, so it may be a misfit at low light of curves that share one
$\theta$ (each single fit had its own) rather than noise of the instrument; the data
cannot tell the two apart. With one random effect, the differences in shape dominated the
deviations and hid this pattern.

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall: the variance model depends on the model of the mean"}
The deviations of the measurements contain everything that the model of the mean leaves
out. A comparison of variance models is only informative once the curve and the random
effects describe the measurements well.
:::

The ratios with two random effects and the exponential standard deviation (the best of
the three by AIC), with Wald intervals, next to those of the main model:

```{r}
main_ratios = rbind(main_answer$ratios$alpha, main_answer$ratios$pmax)
answer_2re = data.frame(
  ratio = c(paste("alpha", comparisons), paste("p_max", comparisons)),
  estimate = ratios_2re, lower = lower_2re, upper = upper_2re,
  main_estimate = main_ratios$estimate, main_lower = main_ratios$lower,
  main_upper = main_ratios$upper
)
show_table(answer_2re)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
change_2re = max(abs(answer_2re$estimate - answer_2re$main_estimate))
```

The ratios change by at most `r f2(change_2re)`, and the intervals hardly change. This is
the model a researcher would probably prefer, as it describes the curves much better. For
students, the model with one random effect gives the same answer, and this section shows
what it misses.

# Checking the estimator by simulation {#sec-simulation}

We draw 300 hypothetical samples of 27 curves from the main model (same plants, treatments
and light levels) and fit each from the same starting values as the data. We keep the log
ratios of $p_{\max}$ and $\alpha$ (estimates and standard errors).

```{r}
set.seed(seed = 1928)
n_samples = 300
sim_estimate = matrix(NA, nrow = n_samples, ncol = 8)
sim_se = matrix(NA, nrow = n_samples, ncol = 8)
n_failed = 0
for (i in seq_len(n_samples)) {
  sim_data = main_data
  sim_data$P = main_obj$simulate(main_fit$par)$P
  sim = fit_photo(sim_data, main_start)
  n_failed = n_failed + (sim$fit$convergence != 0)
  sim_report = summary(sdreport(sim$obj), select = "report")
  rows = rownames(sim_report) %in% c("log_ratio_pmax", "log_ratio_alpha")
  sim_estimate[i, ] = sim_report[rows, "Estimate"]
  sim_se[i, ] = sim_report[rows, "Std. Error"]
}
n_failed
```

The bias, the standard deviation of the estimates, the mean standard error and the
coverage of the 95% Wald interval for each log ratio:

```{r}
main_report = summary(main_sd, select = "report")
used_rows = rownames(main_report) %in% c("log_ratio_pmax", "log_ratio_alpha")
log_ratio_used = main_report[used_rows, "Estimate"]
used_matrix = matrix(log_ratio_used, nrow = n_samples, ncol = 8, byrow = TRUE)
covered = abs(sim_estimate - used_matrix) < critical_value * sim_se
sim_summary = data.frame(
  ratio = paste(rep(c("alpha", "p_max"), each = 4), comparisons),
  bias = colMeans(sim_estimate) - log_ratio_used,
  sd_estimates = apply(sim_estimate, 2, sd),
  mean_se = colMeans(sim_se),
  coverage = colMeans(covered)
)
show_table(sim_summary, digits = 3)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
low_coverage = sim_summary[sim_summary$coverage < 0.925, ]
se_ratio = sim_summary$mean_se / sim_summary$sd_estimates
```

`r if (n_failed == 0) "Every fit converged." else paste(n_failed, "fits did not converge.")`
The biases are small compared with the standard errors (at most
`r f3(max(abs(sim_summary$bias)))` on the log scale). The mean standard errors are
`r round(100 * (1 - max(se_ratio)))`% to `r round(100 * (1 - min(se_ratio)))`% smaller
than the standard deviations of the estimates, and the coverages lie between
`r f1(100 * min(sim_summary$coverage))`% and `r f1(100 * max(sim_summary$coverage))`%,
compared with the range of about 92.5% to 97.5% that 300 samples give for a coverage of
95%. `r if (nrow(low_coverage) > 0) paste0("Below that range are ", paste(paste0(low_coverage$ratio, " (", f1(100 * low_coverage$coverage), "%)"), collapse = "; "), ".") else "None is below that range."`
So with five curves in most combinations the Wald intervals of the ratios are roughly
right under the model but somewhat too narrow for some ratios: the lowest coverages
(`r paste(sim_summary$ratio[order(sim_summary$coverage)[1:2]], collapse = "; ")`)
are closer to 90% than to 95%. @sec-serial explains what this
check cannot see: the samples are simulated with independent deviations within curves and
a common $\sigma_{\mathrm{curve}}$, which the real curves do not have
(@sec-sd-combination).

# Summary: alternatives, pitfalls and teaching notes {#sec-summary}

**Answer.** Plants grown at 28 °C have a typical maximum rate of photosynthesis
`r round(100 * (1 - ra$pmax$estimate[1]))`% lower than plants grown at 22 °C when both are
watered (ratio `r with_interval(ra$pmax[1, ])`), and a lower initial slope, with a similar
dark respiration. A week of drought hardly changes the light response of plants grown at
22 °C, but lowers the maximum rate of plants grown at 28 °C by
`r round(100 * (1 - ra$pmax$estimate[4]))`% and halves their initial slope; the plants at
28 °C differ greatly in how much drought affected them, so much that with a separate
variation among plants for each combination the interval of the drought effect on their
maximum rate is `r with_interval(sra$pmax[4, ])` (@sec-sd-combination). The curvature
$\theta$ is poorly determined (`r theta_lower` to `r f2(theta_ci[["upper"]])`), and
$p_{\max}$ lies beyond the measured light range. A second random effect per curve
describes the curves far better and gives the same ratios.

**Pitfalls.**

1. The column `T` hides R's `TRUE` (@sec-data).
2. The information about the treatments comes from 27 curves, five in three of the four
   combinations (@sec-design).
3. Respiration is extrapolated from 25 µmol/m²/s to darkness (@sec-low-light).
4. The spread among curves grows with the flux, but it is the variation among plants, not
   the measurement error (@sec-spread-among).
5. The textbook formula of the non-rectangular hyperbola loses precision as $\theta$
   approaches zero (@sec-curve-functions).
6. Fits of single curves collapse to a flat curve from common starting values, more often
   with a small starting standard deviation (@sec-one-curve).
7. $\theta$ goes to the boundary in single curves and when it depends on the treatments
   (@sec-single-parameters, @sec-choices).
8. $p_{\max}$ is an extrapolation that depends on the curve (@sec-pmax).
9. The deviations within a curve are correlated (`r f2(serial_cor)`, @sec-serial),
   because a single random effect cannot describe differences in shape.
10. The plants of HT-D differ much more among themselves than those of HT-C and LT-D; a
    common standard deviation among curves gives intervals that are too narrow for
    comparisons with HT-D (@sec-sd-combination).
11. The variance model can only be judged once the mean is right (@sec-two-re).
12. Whether drought was more severe in some batches cannot be separated from the variation
    among plants (@sec-batches, @sec-batch).
13. The Wald intervals of some ratios cover less than 95% under the model, with five curves
    per combination (@sec-simulation).

**Alternatives.**

- The saturating exponential (worse by `r round(mono_gap)` AIC units; @sec-choices).
- A random effect on $p_{\max}$ only or on the gross rate (@sec-choices).
- A standard deviation that changes with the expected rate (@sec-choices, @sec-two-re).
- The additive model without interaction (@sec-candidates).
- The batch as a block (@sec-batch).
- A standard deviation among curves for each combination (@sec-sd-combination; better by
  AIC).
- Two random effects per curve (@sec-two-re; beyond Chapter 7).
- Rates inside the data as the answer, such as the typical net rate at 1000 µmol/m²/s,
  which `ADREPORT()` already gives (@sec-pmax).

**Teaching notes (possible questions for students).**

- Read starting values from the figures: the initial slope and respiration from the first
  two points, the asymptote above the highest rates.
- Derive the numerically stable form of the non-rectangular hyperbola and check it against
  the textbook form.
- Show that multiplying $\alpha$ and $p_{\max}$ by the same factor multiplies the gross
  rate by that factor, and explain why this makes the random effect on the net curve a
  natural choice.
- Compare the random effect on $p_{\max}$ with the one on the whole net curve, with
  @fig-spread-among as the reason.
- Report the ratios with intervals and explain what "the effect of drought depends on the
  growth temperature" means in terms of the interaction.
- Compare $p_{\max}$ from the two curves and explain why it differs while the rates at
  1000 µmol/m²/s agree.
